reviews.text: This game is simply marvelous. Inkshade is a rogue-lite that oozes darkness, mystery, and spectacle. What seemed to be a spiritual successor to Inscryption, Inkshade proves itself to be a completely unique experience of its own. The main similarities between the two being the 'demonic, otherworldly narrator that wants you to play their game' gimmick and the escape room type puzzle that is laid out before you to solve in between rounds. On any given run you will select your path and encounter a very sizable amount of enemy types, special events, lore exposition, and loot; all laid out on a beautiful map for you to navigate. Anyone who has played STS or Inscryption should be familiar with this style of level advancement. The runs start out slow but the main element here that really attracts me is the meta-progression and intense strategy involved while in combat. Moving pieces around and determining the best course of action can sometimes be a very methodical exercise in troop allocation and prudence but you're always rewarded for it when your plan comes to fruition. In between games you upgrade your troops using the currency (Scrim) that you earn in your runs, making for a very addicting loop of going as far as you can in a run so you can upgrade your troops as much as possible to make your next run last even longer. The currency you obtain in your runs starts out a little slow but I assure you that as you progress further it starts to snowball and the game starts to become really quite generous in divvying out your upgrade points. Inkshade definitely has a steep difficulty curve after you progress a little bit so be prepared to lose a lot. Inkshade really wants you to learn from your mistakes, upgrade your troops, explore every nook and cranny of the creaky, haunted ship, and come back to the board a more knowledgeable and prepared adventurer. They really went to great lengths to craft such a detailed experience within the escape room as well; with secrets galore to discover, puzzles that are fun and challenging (but not excruciatingly so), and tidbits of lore sprinkled throughout as you interact with the environment. The actual combat itself reminds me a lot of Into the Breach, so if you like that game's strategical mechanics of combat; then Inkshade will feel familiar to fans of that style's gameplay. It's not for everyone, especially if you're not patient enough to min-max rewards from fights or just don't enjoy strategy games in general however, I love it. Along each of the three main paths you must choose, each one features so, so many different locales and aesthetics; all lovingly adorned with charming animations and adorable set pieces and troops. Even when replaying the same boards across your many runs, the environments are always nice to look at and never seem to lose their allure. I will say that the game might need some performance optimizations, especially around the boss encounters as I noticed some slight dips in FPS and overall performance in those areas due to the amount of elements present. In addition to this suggestion, I would also recommend to the devs taking a look at some of the darkest shadows in the game as it kind of strains your eyes to look at in some parts. This can be ameliorated a bit by messing with the gamma and shadow settings but it isn't the most optimal fix. *UPDATE: On the northern 2nd tier boss, upon loading the fight my game froze entirely for about 30 seconds and then resumed normally. I also have had one CTD in about 10 hours of gameplay. Also when messing with the lower shadow settings, it appears to sometimes create strange lighting artifacts on the playing boards. Aside from the very few complaints I have, the gameplay has been top tier in my opinion. The atmosphere is absolutely immersive, the sound design and music is enchanting, and the narrator's dialogue and presence is wonderfully executed. This game is exactly what I was looking for to be honest and it is exactly what it advertises itself to be; a beautiful and addicting rogue-lite with an incredibly inspired art direction. It is an enthralling experience to say the least and it was 100% worth the long time I waited for it to release.
Strongly recommend!

I put in around a dozen hours into the demo and thoroughly enjoyed my time, enough so that I felt the game was (and still is!) worth every penny. It is best played with the sound on so you can really immerse yourself in the environment. It is, so far, a masterpiece. Part rogue-like, part turn based strategy, part point and click adventure with puzzle solving.
Storyteller took one look at me, smacked me out the game for touching too much. 10/10 Emotional Damage. Buyers be aware.
I'm glad someone was willing to make an Inscryption sequel. I wish the game wasn't so short and the combat wasn't so simple and unambitious, though.

I really wanted to like this game. Inscryption is one of my favorite games and this nails the tone and vibe of the world. However, the gameplay mechanics are just not there. I love a challenging roguelike but this is really just grindy more than skillful. It will be IMPOSSIBLE for you to win a run or even get close without HEAVILY grinding the meta currency to level up the characters. I could have completely missed the mark here and maybe there are mechanics that make the game more strategic down the road but there is very little instructions or tooltips that assist to make it enjoyable getting to that point.

The theming of the game is heavily inspired by inscription, a game I love, so I had high hopes coming into this. But the gameplay loop is just... boring? Maybe (?) the game is balanced around permanent upgrades and it is expected that runs kill you early so you can upgrade the characters you have? Or maybe there is some "trick" to combat that somehow allows you to defeat enemy clusters twice as big as yours. Anyway, I didn't find it fun and can't be bothered to grind for hours in the hopes that it may become fun later.

I enjoyed the design of the base rogue-lite game and upgrading pieces for the tactics-style gameplay. But... The game itself is just too dark and the walkable area is a mess. The board can be thematically dark, which is a cool idea in theory. It instead leads to frustration and confusion when you can't SEE anything. Something as simple as identifying which piece of yours is which is not a difficulty I was hoping for when playing a tactics game.
I'm enjoying Inkshade! Very clearly a love letter to the Inscryption format. Vibes are good, I love the change to tactics, gameplay is sharp.
This game is an Inscription clone that is easily better than Inscription.

The gameplay starts off lacking in strategy, but as you unlock more interesting units, it improves significantly. Unfortunately to unlock characters you have to brave the very spooky rooms. I'm not a horror game player, but luckily my girlfriend is, so I got her to do most of the room exploration :/ There aren't actually any jumpscares in the game, so if you are a wimp like myself, you can go through it knowing nothing will jump out at you

I want to love this but I think it needs work. I don't love how the characters need to be upgraded before they can be decent units. It makes me feel like I just need to play the game a lot to farm the xp to make the units better, to progress more. I love inscryption, so i love the style and feel of the game, but i think inscryption is so simple that it makes it easy to get into. This is also simple and easy to understand, but its not hooking me. It doesn't feel like I'm solving the gameplay loop and trying to get good at it. It felt like I understood I needed to farm XP to make my weak units strong, and I just didn't care enough to do that. I would revisit this game if it had a big rebalancing, which is asking a lot. Nice presentation, didn't hook me as much as I hoped. I think the gameplay and user experience needs a bit more work.

For as far as I got, there doesn't seem to be much more to the core gameplay loop than the basic unit stats. There's nothing really that sets units apart aside from a basic stat being slightly higher, and I can see a long term problem with this game being investing heavily into one unit and then that single unit carrying the game and making you wish you didn't pick up any other figurines to clutter your potential rewards with. The opponents decision making is incredibly bare bones making the gameplay pretty non-challenging and unrewarding; it's a simple tactic to just lure enemies away one at a time and dogpile them individually. I don't really have much hope that either of these things will change if I get further into the game. A lot of people compare this to Inscryption; and aesthetically, it is, I suppose. But it seems many forget that there's a lot more to a game than aesthetics. I wouldn't recommend this to anybody looking for a similar experience; it is it's own thing, for better or worse

I was hoping for a clever tactical experience, like Into the Breach, XCOM, or Darkest Dungeon. Instead the combat is just completely boring. It's mathematically impossible to beat until you've upgraded your units a lot. Every combat is just a pure stat-check of whether or not you have enough HP to aggro enemy units one at a time. I have no interest in investing hours into the metacurrency just so that I don't automatically lose battles. At one point I was able to get a ranged unit to attack downhill without getting hit back. That's about it for strategy.

TLDR: Not a true roguelike, very grindy and limited strategy. + The 3d hidden object / puzzle metagame is fun and creepy. + The graphics are nice, although a little too obscured by too much darkness. - This game relies on meta progression and no mater how good and lucky you are you will be playing many times to upgrade your characters. This is unlike the best rouges e.g. Hades or Slay the spire which may be extremely hard but not impossible to win on early runs. - As you upgrade your meta the enemy also upgrades. More units, more health. This means you spend longer grinding. - Some characters are just bad , they will never be good. This cuts down on viable strategy. - Putting aside the meta problems the strategy is fairly basic relying on positioning and basic stats there are very few synergys or fun combos. Whilst this might be OK for a time, the game-play does not stand up to this level of grind. - Mutations / upgrades etc are also fairly basic and boring. Could be much improved relatively simply by reducing the grind.

"Where the heck am I?" "Why is there a demon with a snarky attitude inviting me to boardgame night?" "Did that statue just turn its head when I wasn't looking?" Poke and fiddle with everything, annoy the GM, solve riddles, find gaming pieces in unexpected places. What's not to like?

Fun game. Would've liked the main campaign to be longer or there being a hard mode to use all the OP pieces without feeling like you are cheating the game. Also a bit sad that you created this really spooky world, but then there being no real consequences for your actions. But yeah, enjoyed the experience and definitely think it's worth the price. Haven't completed all achievements or challenge modes yet. So let's see how they feel.

There's a good game in here, but it needs a couple polish passes still, to develop it further. I'm reviewing this late September; I'm hopeful that in a few months this will BE a good game. The bones are there. The models are artful, the villain design is clever. Solid marks for visual design of the pieces and boards. The core concept is charming. There are two things that are really holding this game back: 1) SUPER HARSH lighting, that goes from glare to total blackness in a handspan's distance. This is a game that wants you to wander around and explore, but just existing in the environment is unpleasant and disorienting because the light goes from blindingly bright to impenetrable darkness constantly. This is a whole world of overpowering spotlights in otherwise black space, with no ambient light whatsoever. 2) The core gameplay loop goes from frustratingly impossible to trivially easy very suddenly, with very little sense of progression in between. There's a pacing you want to set, with a rogue-like like this, where you're making more progress each time, give or take. In Inkshade, you barely make any progress for several games when you first start, making frustratingly short run after frustratingly short run, and earning very little upgrade credits while you re-explore the same content loop after loop until you discover the 2 or 3 upgrades that are currently OP. Then the difficulty goes to almost zero for the next half of the game as all the clever play skills you had to learn become unimportant, and you simply overpower the antagonists with no need for tactics. I suspect there'ssome balancing that could be done by making some of the early characters even cheaper to upgrade, while keeping their max stats limited enough to make them dead ends, only useful for getting you to make longer runs to earn more. Also, the armor upgrades are FAR too binary right now. Even a single point of armor lets you ignore more than half the enemies on the field. If armor wore down and only reset at the end of the turn, but was cheaper and more plentiful, that would keep you from simply tanking minor characters: Getting swarmed would still be a threat and more clever play would still be important.
its gorgeous but i found it somewhat tactically shallow and relying more on roguelite progression than skill progression, which isnt objectively bad but is not to my taste

At first, the wolves are scary, then the sorcerers are scary, then the executioner is scary, then the main bosses are scary, then suddenly every encounter is manageable in a way that truly feels like you've mastered the game, and then you're travelling through the northern winds and... yeah it gets scary again. 10/10 would annoy the abyssal creature by touching everything again.

not much of a rogue-like when the enemies scale with your progress... i got to the point where i thought i understood the mechanics and was making a better team, and then the early map encounters got upgraded. Seemed kinda cheap, but i thought it was at least linked to the amount of money I had spent, so I started a new game to try again with this new knowledge. I bought defense upgrades right off the back for my team, knowing this would be optimal, and then ran into the same upgraded 'random' encounters on literally the second run of a new game. Kinda ruins the fun for me knowing it is just artificially making the game difficult no matter what choices I make.

I picked up this game because I was looking for a [b]turn based tactics[/b] game to try. The visual style of this was excellent, and the chess like pieces pretty suggested to me a balance between chess and, say, XCOM or Final Fantasy Tactics. Perfect. I could also see that the narrator/opponent was a character, not just changing each battle or faceless. That's fine, but not something that grabbed my interest any extra. Once I picked up the game I saw that the tactical board game is also mixed with a bit of [b]deck-building[/b]. So the pieces i have to play with each match are a bit randomized. Ok, that's fine by me and might even be an excellent addition to the gameplay mix. I like a reasonable bit of chaos and I'm willing to try it. Then the game adds a layer of [b]roguelike[/b], where I fail the first couple runs and unlock the ability to spend coins earned in battle to upgrade my units. Hmm. Normally that would be rewarding persistence and giving me time to learn better skills, but here it just feels like I'm expected to grind to advance. That's not great. Oh, and the world outside the board game is a puzzle room, and maybe an [b]escape room[/b] game. I can't say I'm very interested in that. I just wanted to play the board game. But [b]gaining new board pieces is locked behind the escape room, and the escape room is locked behind advancing in the board game[/b]? No, I don't like that at all. And then there's a final addition to the mix: there's [b]power scaling of the enemies[/b]. So I'm not even necessarily rewarded for grinding to advance, I might be punished if I do it wrong. Maybe it's trying to be a [b]RPG (?)[/b] element, but it doesn't feel like it here. It just feels like it's trying to do to much at once and I can't tell if there's much of a core left in the board game. The AI seems to just charge at the weakest unit in range and sit passively waiting if there's nothing in range. The units don't seem to have that much variety; it's just elaborate paper rock scissors in a way, except here it's magic, ranged, melee. It still looks beautiful, and feels like it has potential, but it's just not the game for me unless I find a mod for some different units. It's trying to mix too many things together instead of focusing on a solid core.
Inscription, but worse, nonetheless enjoyable, although very grindy in the mid/late game

I really want to like this game. It has the foundation of a good game. But hour after hour, I don't feel like I'm doing anything but grinding towards piece upgrades. I keep hoping I get to a point where my use of clever tactics and skill will be the determining factor of success of failure. But game after game, the overwhelmingly important factor is how many upgrades have I bought so far. Die to the same fight a couple times no matter what I do. Use the money to buy an upgrade. Now the fight is completely trivial no matter what I do. Move on to the next fight where it's the same situation. Deeply disappointing.

To any Inscryption player looking at this thinking it can scratch that itch, There is a fundamental flaw in the game design that you can very simply generalize as: (Inscryption but there is no sigils). To go into detail of what I mean by this, the game plays like a turn based chess (Something like Heroes of might and magic 3) but it provides no interesting build potential to its chess pieces. Every piece in the game basically boils down to 5 basic attributes, that being Movement, Health, Attack range, Damage and Defense.(Which is standard for any game Mostly) And that is it. You can only modify these five aspects of your pieces, there are two types of damages that is countered by two types of defenses and this ratio is literally 1:1 so if your piece has 1 basic attack and tries to attack a piece that has 1 basic armor it will deal 0 damage. - This leads to a problem of not having anything fun or creative to make or cook up, because there is literally no variable or effect to add besides just changing the numbers of those 5 basic stats. So mostly all the pieces of the game feel exactly the same aside from a few exceptions of having super long range or super high damage but that isn't super FUN. - The other problem with Gameplay is the AI, it will simply never move except only when one of its pieces is in range of yours. Combined with what I mentioned about attacks and armor in this game it leads to the gameplay loop of leading your HIGH defense unit just one tile in range of an enemy that Can't break its defense and then ending your turn, after which the one piece will charge out of position and deal nothing and you can swarm him. And That is it, That is literally-Fundamentally the Most Optimal play for the whole gameplay for every combat encounter. - Another unacceptably boring part of the game is Upgrading your pieces, you can do this at any time outside of combat by gold you gain from playing the board, Upgrades are for a "Piece Type" meaning that if you upgrade your "Cultist Piece" every "Cultist Piece" you will ever find will also have all of those upgrades. Now it doesn't sound that bad by itself but the real ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ WTF Kicker is the fact that the enemy chess pieces LITERALLY Increase in Strength based on your OWN Upgrades even On the same Previous Battle Encounters! This leads to a psychological feedback loop of Why the ♥♥♥♥ Do I even bother upgrading anything if the enemy pieces also upgrade?? Its not like you get anything enjoyable besides Increasing those 5 basic stats which won't even matter since all the enemy pieces will also increase those same 5 basic stats. - I genuinely tried to enjoy the game because its visuals and design are great and clearly a lot of work went into the atmosphere and delivery, however the gameplay is just Poorly thought out and Its simply BORING. No matter how clever you are in writing or beautiful in your art, if a game is Literally Boring then it really will just overshadow everything else when it comes to being a video game..

This game is closer to cookie clicker, but without the numbers going up. It's not really satisfying to play, and its really stressful. I love everything but the core gameplay loop. This game you are expected to upgrade pieces to be able to get farther into the map, but then you lose a piece for the rest of that run and get one that you don't have upgraded during the run. That case is effectively a lose at that point. And with the grindy nature of the game, and the long runs, it's super unfun for me. I'm only just over 2 hours, and it feels like I'm already doing the same thing over and over again. This isn't like chest for skill, and it's not like Inscription for replayablity. And this is a game of many replays. Edit: - I just decided to reset so I can focus on one character to upgrade, and the reset did reset my progress, but there are still additional enemies so now I'm kinda soft-locked on a harder mode with no upgrades.

Inkshade, a solid 6/10 The first couple hours of the game is by far the most enjoyable as you are getting use to the systems and the fact you can upgrade your pieces mid run prevents restarting runs just because you think you cant progress without upgrades. Not a puzzle game at all though, the puzzles are simplistic and dont require much thought at all bar one. The game is too dark, like i get why parts of it is dark and it is a good addition to the gameplay but the fact my pieces aren't visible in the darkness is just annoying. It doesn't result in me not playing them it just results in me scanning the screen with my mouse. The gameplay feels redundant near the end as there isn't many layers to the gameplay, get a tank and a ranged unit and you've won. I would of liked more use out of the map aswell, the question marks 9 times out of 10 were just lore points masqueraded as random encounters. I genuinely dont know why you do elite encounters, whenever i did them it was just harder for no noticeable reward. TLDR, Fun mix between Fire emblems character permadeath, general gameplay and inscryptions deck building. The game is not a puzzle game and you wont find engaging puzzles within while playing. But it overstays its welcome as it doesn't add new layers to gameplay as you progress.

Pretty solid game; it takes very heavily from inscription and many others in the genre, but ultimately I thought it was pretty fun – but I was expecting a bit more. The game's progression can be fairly repetitive, and unfortunately the game is not very well optimized so even my fairly powerful system took a toll on some of the maps, leaving me a little dissatisfied. In comparison to Inscryption it has its own spin and does have its own thing going. The problem is the story falls short by a fair margin. The character connections are void, and the ending in my opinion was pretty unfulfilling. Ultimately though, it wasn’t terrible. I say this because I don't have any recommendation as to how the story should have gone. If I ever do I will revisit this review. I guess one redeeming addition to this game would be a kaycee’s mod equivalent. I think some more material into a backstory or some type extension into the play, or even a community extension to self build maps for other players to try could be fun. The game is fun; if you haven’t played Inscryption I would recommend that first. I give credit to the game mechanics that were original and fun; ultimately I would just like to see some more tweaks to what could be a very impressive game, but then again the genre is pretty hard to beat.
I don't think it's possible for me to dislike a Fire Emblem and Inscryption crossover set in a really cool world

Wonderfully crafted game. Tone, setting, and vibes are all in place, and lots of passion is seen everywhere. Pacing can be slow at times, but that's one of the two only real issues I see with the game. The other issue is how often it crashes. I crash about 2-3 times a session, which is super annoying. Also, if you look at your crew, it's almost a 100% chance to crash. It's not required at all to look at them, so this is passable as a crash. It is quick to open the game back up and continue where you left off though, which makes the crashing more of an annoyance than anything. Otherwise, absolutely wonderful game. I have had a lot of fun playing!
10/10 Play this till the end, Its is an incredible story with a great plot twist ending.

Okay, so, I picked this game up because it looked pretty interesting and I enjoyed the demo. Obvious parallels to Inscyption aside, I was willing to give it an honest try on its own terms (because I hated the story of Inscryption). The story of Inkshade kind of hits you over the head to where I feel it would have been better if the Narrator used 'The Captain' instead of 'You' when playing the board game. Sort of bury the lead. By the time we get to the end, we've gotten the point. Thoroughly. The exploration aspect was fun, but the video settings which I never got the hang of ended with moving around the ship giving me motion sickness. Which I suppose is an interesting bit of immersion if I'm getting seasickness playing a game about walking around a ship. Lastly, and I know it's sort of the point, the gameplay board was obscured in darkness and scenery to where I couldn't see my own units' stats or even where they WERE often times. Plus, being able to move the board only so far, I ended up misclicking more often than I was comfortable with- ending turns prematurely, attacking the wrong targets, etc. I know I could tilt and rotate the playspace, but it ended up feeling really clumsy. I would have also liked to see more units with different abilities, perhaps buffing others, AoE, more than just varying degrees of the same seven stats. ALL OF THAT HAVING BEEN SAID. I really did enjoy playing Inkshade. It gave me pretty much exactly what I wanted, and aside from those bits of criticism, it didn't deliberately insult me like Inscryption, Eiyuden Chronicle or Artifact Adventure. I could see myself coming back to Inkshade again and again, especially if I could manage to figure out the aforementioned technical issues.

Its rare i play a game that i enjoy every part of. This one comes really really close. I love the aesthetic, the dark shadowy eldritch like aspect is a favorite of mine. The music is catchy, and didnt feel old even at the end. The puzzles arent too hard, and you can certainly solve all of them without a guide, id say the hardest is probably the candle puzzle in the first unlocked room, atleast for me. The combat at no point felt unfair, there is minimal RNG, so when i did lose it always felt that i was having a skill issue, or didnt play optimally. towards the end of the game you can get units so strong they almost singlehandedly sweep stages, i never felt the need to grind or anything of the sort. You should play this game if you like RPGs, if you like eldritch horror, Inscryption, or you like D&D.

Some of the most fun I have had playing a game. The combat is unique, challenging and not too grindy. Late game you can get into a rhythm and feel like you are unstoppable, then the finale hits. I love the puzzles and the storytelling. The models and world building are beautiful. I only wish there was more after the finale. If you ever make a sequel or DLC that would be amazing!

This is a pretty game that is extremely shallow and endlessly tedious. The aesthetic is clearly trying to imitate Inscryption, but it lacks the charm of Inscryption in favor of having the game master talk incessantly while saying almost nothing interesting. The gameplay loop is a simple tactics game that also lacks any interesting twists. Units are solely differentiated by their stats with only a couple of them having abilities, so the entire strategy is just to find the most upgradable unit and upgrade it as much as you can so it's unstoppable. The way that attack and defense stats work means that it's very easy to build a unit that can one shot every enemy while they can do no damage to you. This is very easy to set up and trivializes the game, but if you don't realize this and spend your initial upgrade money in other ways then you'll have to spend ages grinding that money back up while you have nearly useless units until you reach the threshold of becoming unstoppable. There are also implied mechanics that never pay off. The entire game is super dark and some units carry lamps, but the light only determines how hard it is for you to see pieces. You'll never find an enemy that is scared of light or anything like that. The shallow aesthetics are neat, but there's not much past that.
